Advantage

An action's value $q_\pi(s,a)$ mixes two things: how good the state is, and how good the action is within it. The advantage $q_\pi(s,a) - v_\pi(s)$ keeps only the second. It is the score a policy gradient should use: positive means better than the policy's usual behaviour here, negative means worse.

Better or worse than usual?

The slippery corridor from Lesson 75: $-1$ per step, 20% of moves slip, $\gamma = 1$. The policy moves right with probability $p$ in every cell. Bars are the exact advantages of ← and → in each cell. Click a cell to see the numbers.

The values $q$ and $v$ are large and negative everywhere, because every cell is several steps from the flag. The advantages are small, and they carry the only information the policy needs. Set $p = 0.95$: moving right is now what the policy usually does, so its advantage shrinks towards zero, while going left is sharply negative.

Estimating it from one step

The agent never sees $q_\pi$. With a correct critic, the TD error $\delta = R + \hat v(S') - \hat v(s)$ after taking $a$ in $s$ is an unbiased estimate of the advantage. Uses the selected cell.

The maths

The advantage function of policy $\pi$ is

$$A_\pi(s,a) = q_\pi(s,a) - v_\pi(s)$$

It measures how much better it is to take $a$ in $s$ (and then follow $\pi$) than to just follow $\pi$ from $s$.

Average advantage is zero. Since $v_\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\, q_\pi(s,a)$ (Lesson 23),

$$\sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\, A_\pi(s,a) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\, q_\pi(s,a) - v_\pi(s) \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) = v_\pi(s) - v_\pi(s) = 0$$

Under the policy's own probabilities, the actions are on average exactly "as usual". So some must be above zero and some below, unless all are zero. The third line of numbers above checks this.

The policy gradient with advantages. Taking $b(s) = v_\pi(s)$ in Lesson 74's baseline result gives

$$\nabla J(\boldsymbol\theta) \propto \mathbb{E}_\pi\big[A_\pi(S_t, A_t)\, \nabla \ln \pi(A_t \mid S_t, \boldsymbol\theta)\big]$$

Each action's log-probability moves in proportion to its advantage. The value of the state no longer enters.

Estimating it. With $\hat v = v_\pi$, the TD error is an unbiased sample:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) - v_\pi(S_t) \,\big|\, S_t = s, A_t = a\big] = q_\pi(s,a) - v_\pi(s) = A_\pi(s,a)$$

The first term's expectation is $q_\pi(s,a)$ by the Bellman equation for $q_\pi$ (Lesson 26). In the corridor, $\delta$ takes one value if the move succeeds and another if it slips, and the running average settles on the bar's height. Lesson 77 plugs $\delta$ into the gradient; Lesson 78 builds better estimates from several steps.
